chapter: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
title: Feeling at home again and the bass trombone
summary: His sound was a plus with Duke; the 1960s section was Chuck Connors and Buster Cooper, and bass trombone came into bands.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: But you felt good about your peculiar sound once you were back in Duke's band?
Well, it's like coming home. I mean it didn't worry you that your sound was alien to -- to the rest of them.
Well, your sound was distinctive
rather --
Well, that's not good where you have an organized band such as CBS.
But it was a decided plus with Duke and Ellington for you as a soloist.
Well, it was all right, I guess.
Then after -- you were with Duke then from 1963 through until --
-- until 1970.
January in '70.
During that time what -- who else worked in the trombone section? Let's see. Chuck Connors.
Oh, yes. Chuck Connors and Buster Cooper.
And Buster came in what -- it was in '62 -- early in '62. And, oh -- Lew Blackburn was there briefly.
Right. That's right. Lew Blackburn. He was in Europe, wasn't he?
I don't know. I haven't seen any of these -- quite a few of these fellows in years.
Was Chuck Connors the first to play bass trombone?
Right.
In the band? How did that come about,

Well, the -- the bass trombone became prominent in all bands I remember just before I left CBS. They were looking for a bass trombone. And I -- that's the first time that I'd heard they were being played outside of symphonies.
Did it give a different feel to you -- to the trombone section to have a bass trombone?

Oh, yes. It gives a good heavy bottom, and I think one of the most prominent developers of the bass trombone in the popular field was a fellow by the name of Roberts. And he's out here in California now still playing bass trombone in the studios and places. Very good. He's a terrific musician.
